newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn coalition parties approve tax-cutting plan.
newsitem.headline: Bonn coalition parties approve tax-cutting plan.

text.p: The coalition parties in Germany's government on Thursday gave their blessing to a big tax-cutting reform plan aimed at boosting the country's competitiveness and putting its four million unemployed back to work.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, hailing the tax reform as the biggest in Germany's post-war history, said it would stimulate investment, speeding the pace of growth and job creation.
Peter Hintze, general secretary of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) went further: "It is the biggest tax reform in German history. It is a reform for the century."

Kohl declared himself "very satisfied". Seeking to silence critics from both within his own party and the opposition, he said they should first come up with "a proposal of this scale which also has such a positive impact on small incomes."

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said the reform would raise German competitiveness. "Our tax reform concept is the most important answer to our economic problems: globalisation, weak investment, unemployment and over-regulation," he said.
Leaders of the CDU and FDP both approved the plan, and its backing was assured by Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU).

After months of damaging coalition wrangling, a tax policy working group finally came up with a two-step plan on Wednesday which would cut 81.9 billion marks ($50 billion) in taxes while scrapping an extra 38.1 billion marks worth of tax breaks.

The resulting tax cuts would be 43.8 billion marks -- more than the government can afford. Waigel wants to raise the 15 percent rate of value-added tax by one point to bring the net relief for taxpayers down to 30 billion marks.

But Kohl's CDU remains split on VAT, with a majority of its leadership wanting a two-point hike to help bail out the social security system. Meanwhile, regional CDU officials -- who face elections soon -- are set against a VAT hike.
Christian Wulff, the CDU leader in Lower Saxony who has criticised plans for the VAT rise and even called for Waigel to resign, said he and Kohl had discussed their differences.
"I am by and large still opposed to an increase in VAT," Wulff told journalists. "I believe the dispute that I triggered was the right thing to do, especially in retrospect."
The CDU put off a VAT decision until February, when Labour Minister Norbert Bluem will finish a pensions reform report.
The tax reform has run into criticism from opposition parties who say it punishes those on middle and low incomes while offering giveaways to the rich.

The package is "a mixture of reform, retouches and tricks," Joachim Poss, finance spokesman of the Social Democrats (SPD) told German Radio. The SPD has threatened to veto a VAT rise using its blocking majority in parliament's upper house.
The plan's main points look like this: Incomes below 13,000 marks for single earners would be tax-free from 1999. Pay up to 18,000 marks would be taxed at 15 percent.
Then, a sliding scale running from 22.5 percent comes into force, hitting a top rate of 39 percent at 90,000 marks.
The new income tax rates, to take effect in 1999, would cut existing rates running from 26 percent to 53 percent and bring the lion's share of the tax cuts.
The other big tax cut would be a two-step drop in corporate taxation. By 1999, retained profits would be taxed at 35 percent and profits paid out to shareholders at 25 percent.
That is the simple part. A coalition document listed over 70 revenue-sapping tax exemptions which are due for the chop.

The main items are: reducing tax relief on Sunday, holiday and night work; tightening up on companies' chances to hide profits; cutting travel allowances; halving tax-free interest allowances and upping taxes on life insurance and pensions.

Although the coalition parties have agreed on the tax plan, it will have to go through several rounds of horse-trading in Germany's consensus-based political process. Finance Ministry officials said it may not even become law until next year. ($1=1.6383 Mark)
